title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Public comment opens today on Saline data center river discharge amid local pushback.

lines.text: Good morning and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.

It's Friday, July 31, and our big story today is the fresh public comment period that just opened on a permit to discharge treated wastewater from the proposed Saline data center into the Saline River.
Right, Graham. This feels like the latest flashpoint in a project that's already drawn plenty of attention over power and land use.
Exactly. The application is tied to the Oracle-OpenAI backed facility in Washtenaw County, and residents downstream are now weighing in on potential changes to water quality and flow.
What do we know so far about how this discharge would actually work?
The filing shows treated wastewater from the facility's cooling systems would go straight into the river after processing. It's the first concrete environmental price tag we've seen on the project.
And locals are already voicing concerns about that, right?

They are. The Sun Times News reports ongoing tensions in the township over infrastructure demands, with residents worried about water usage and quality impacts in an area that already relies on the river for other needs.
This isn't the first time we've seen these kinds of fights in Michigan townships. How does Saline fit into the bigger pattern?

It's part of a wave of proposals where hyperscale projects land in rural or semi-rural spots. We've seen similar pushback elsewhere over farmland conversion and road strain, but water is the new flashpoint here because of the river discharge request.
Who are the main players pushing this one forward?
The companies behind the massive proposed facility near Saline filed the permit. Yesterday MLive noted it puts a direct environmental cost on the table after earlier scrutiny on power and land.
And power is still a huge piece, isn't it?
It is. The project is expected to draw heavily on the electric grid, which ties into yesterday's comments from Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.
What did he say on C-SPAN?
He criticized the plan over expected grid and water strain, arguing that tax breaks and infrastructure costs would hit Michigan residents while benefits flow elsewhere.
That sharpens the debate right before the August primary, doesn't it?
It does. The remarks highlight how these projects can become campaign issues when local resources are on the line.
What about electric bills specifically? How might this affect ratepayers?

Large data centers can increase overall demand, which often leads to higher costs passed along unless new generation or efficiency measures keep pace. The Saline filing doesn't detail exact numbers, but it's the kind of load that planners watch closely.
And water usage beyond the discharge?

Cooling systems at these scales pull significant volumes. The permit focuses on what goes back into the river after treatment, but upstream withdrawal is part of the same conversation residents are having.
Farmland and towns — how does this project intersect with those?
The site is in a township setting where preserving open land has been a priority. Adding a major facility can shift tax bases and traffic patterns, which is why local zoning fights keep popping up.
What happens next with this permit?
The public comment window is open now. Officials will review input before deciding on approval, which could set precedents for similar requests in other river-adjacent sites.
Any sense of how long that process might take?
State environmental reviews like this typically run several weeks to months depending on comments received and any required studies.
Meanwhile, there's also the District C county council race heating up over these exact issues.
Yes, both contenders in that southwest Michigan district say local rules aren't ready for large AI projects and want a pause while the county studies power demand and zoning.
That could set the tone for other townships, right?
It could. The race is being watched as a bellwether for how communities balance growth with resource limits.
Shifting to quick hits, another story from yesterday involves Michigan residents getting a chance to hear power, jobs, and tax details at an August session.
That's right. The public event will outline a proposed project and its local impacts, giving neighbors direct answers before decisions move forward.
And in Shelby, a court ruled on the data center annexation fight.
A judge issued a decision on whether the site can bypass county oversight. Macomb County residents now have clearer rules on future approvals and potential tax revenue.
Over in Cass County, residents are organizing to shape future rules.
Local groups are preparing zoning changes after the Dowagiac project to protect farmland and roads. County decisions will determine how much industrial load the area accepts.
A hyperscale company sold Bitcoin to fund its Michigan AI campus.
They cashed out 100 BTC to speed construction. Neighbors will see new power lines and tax questions tied to that financing move.
And executives tied to the Saline project donated to Congresswoman Haley Stevens.
The donations raise questions about influence in Washtenaw County as the project advances.
On deck, are there any meetings listeners can attend soon?
The August data center session we mentioned is one to watch — check the Michigan Data Center Tracker for exact dates and locations as they firm up.
Any others popping up this week?
Nothing confirmed beyond that right now, but the tracker is the best spot for real-time updates on township and county sessions.
Sounds good. Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Saline River Permit Opens as Data Center Water Fight Intensifies
